bull.argument: Walmart's filing shows a business compounding at scale with improving fundamentals. Net sales rose 4.7% to $706.4 billion in fiscal 2026, and consolidated net income grew to $22.3 billion from $20.2 billion. Free cash flow reached $14.9 billion, up from $12.7 billion, even while capital expenditures rose to $26.6 billion to fund omnichannel growth. Walmart U.S. comparable sales grew 4.3%, with eCommerce contributing about 4.3 points, showing the digital investment is converting into real sales. Returns remain high, with ROI at 15.1% and ROA at 8.2%. Management is also returning capital: $8.1 billion of buybacks in fiscal 2026, a new $30.0 billion authorization, and a dividend raised to $0.99 from $0.94. The risks the filing lists are real, including tariffs, cyber threats, and AI competition, but they are the same risks any large retailer faces, and the company's AA-rated balance sheet gives it room to absorb them.

claims.claim: Walmart's eCommerce growth is adding materially to comparable sales in its largest segment.
claims.quote: Walmart U.S. eCommerce sales positively contributed approximately 4.3% and 2.9% to comparable sales for fiscal 2026 and 2025, respectively.

claims.claim: Free cash flow improved despite heavier investment spending.
claims.quote: Free cash flow for fiscal 2026 increased when compared to fiscal 2025 due to an increase in cash provided by operating income, lower cash tax payments and timing of certain payments, partially offset by an increase of $2.9 billion in capital expenditures

claims.claim: Management is returning substantial capital to shareholders and has signaled confidence through a larger buyback authorization.
claims.quote: In February 2026, the Board of Directors approved a new $30.0 billion share repurchase authorization, which has no expiration date or other restrictions

bear.argument: The filing shows a company spending heavily to defend its position, with returns under pressure. Capital expenditures rose to $26.6 billion from $23.8 billion, and management says it is allocating most capital to eCommerce, supply chain and automation, yet free cash flow was only $14.9 billion, and ROI fell from 15.5% to 15.1% as invested capital grew. Operating margin declined from 4.4% to 4.2%, and operating income grew only about 1.6%, far slower than the 4.7% sales growth. Management itself warns that eCommerce investments and any operating losses will 'adversely impact our financial performance in the short-term,' and that the benefits may not materialize. Meanwhile, the filing discloses rising self-insured liability costs of about $0.9 billion, a $0.7 billion PhonePe charge, and exposure to numerous antitrust, opioid and wage class actions. Net income was also flattered by a $2.1 billion gain on investments, which is not operating performance. Shareholder payouts of $7.5 billion in dividends and $8.1 billion in buybacks were funded while the working capital deficit widened to $22.6 billion.

claims.claim: Capital spending is rising faster than the returns it generates, with ROI declining as invested capital grows.
claims.quote: The decrease in ROI was primarily due to an increase in average invested capital due to higher purchases of property and equipment.

claims.claim: Management warns that its eCommerce and technology investments will hurt near-term results and may not deliver long-term benefits.
claims.quote: the cost of certain investments in eCommerce, technology, talent and automation, including any operating losses incurred for those initiatives, will adversely impact our financial performance in the short-term

claims.claim: Reported earnings were helped by non-operating investment gains, and operating margin fell.
claims.quote: Other gains and losses resulted in a net gain of $2.1 billion and a net loss of $0.8 billion in fiscal 2026 and 2025, respectively

bull.argument: The bear case leans on real pressures, but it overstates them. Operating income did grow, from $29.3 billion to $29.8 billion, and the $0.9 billion self-insured liability increase and $0.7 billion PhonePe charge are identifiable items that management quantifies, not signs of broken economics. ROI fell only 0.4 points to 15.1%, still a strong return, and the decline was attributed to property purchases, which the filing describes as spending to support omnichannel growth. Management has also been explicit that near-term eCommerce costs are the price of the strategy. The $2.1 billion gain is real but it is non-operating, and the filing's own operating metrics show the core business improving: gross profit rate rose 8 basis points, and Walmart U.S. operating income grew $1.3 billion. Free cash flow still rose to $14.9 billion from $12.7 billion. A working capital deficit is, per the filing, how the company normally operates. The concession is that the margin is thin and the investment payoff is unproven; the case rests on whether comparable-sales growth from eCommerce keeps converting into profit.

claims.claim: Operating income grew even as the bear case emphasized margin pressure, and the core U.S. segment drove it.
claims.quote: Walmart U.S. segment operating income increased $1.3 billion

claims.claim: Free cash flow rose despite the larger capital program, which the filing attributes to lower cash taxes and timing.
claims.quote: Free cash flow for fiscal 2026 increased when compared to fiscal 2025 due to an increase in cash provided by operating income

claims.claim: The working capital deficit reflects the company's normal operating model rather than a liquidity problem.
claims.quote: We generally operate with a working capital deficit due to our efficient use of cash in funding operations

bear.argument: The opponent concedes the decisive point: margins are thin and the payoff from eCommerce spending is unproven. Operating margin fell from 4.4% to 4.2% even as sales grew 4.7%, and operating income grew only about 1.6%, so most of the sales growth did not reach the operating line. The $0.9 billion liability charge and $0.7 billion PhonePe charge are real costs that recur in the reported base, and the filing says rising costs to resolve claims across the industry are a continuing trend. Walmart U.S. operating income rose $1.3 billion on $20.6 billion of added sales, a weak incremental margin. Free cash flow of $14.9 billion is after $26.6 billion of capex, and it is less than the $15.1 billion generated in fiscal 2024, so the cash return on the spending has not improved over two years. Free cash flow was also flattered by lower cash taxes and payment timing, which the filing says is not durable. Dividends and buybacks of $15.6 billion exceeded free cash flow, funded by short-term borrowings that rose to $6.6 billion. The $2.1 billion investment gain is non-operating and cannot be relied on to repeat.

claims.claim: Operating margin declined while sales grew, so the spending is not yet converting into profit.
claims.quote: Operating income as a percentage of net sales 4.2 % 4.4 %

claims.claim: Shareholder payouts exceeded free cash flow, and borrowing rose to cover the gap.
claims.quote: Short-term borrowings as of January 31, 2026 and 2025 were $6.6 billion and $3.1 billion, respectively

claims.claim: Management warns the eCommerce and technology investments will weigh on results in the short term and may not pay off over the long term.
claims.quote: failure to realize the benefits of these investments may adversely impact our financial performance over the longer term

judge.reasoning: The bear side's claims are largely verified and tie directly to margin compression (4.4% to 4.2%), ROI decline, and borrowing to fund shareholder payouts, which the bull only partially rebuts. The bull's key operating-income support rests on a NOT VERIFIED quote, weakening its evidence, though it effectively reframes the bear's charges as identifiable items and points to the unproven payoff as the crux. On balance the bear's verified evidence and its responsiveness to the bull's concession edge out the bull.
